questions.stem: Business analysts who know Power Query need to clean data from a SaaS application each day, with no code to maintain. Which tool fits best?

options.text: Dataflow Gen2
A KQL queryset
A T-SQL stored procedure
A Spark notebook

questions.explanation: Dataflow Gen2 gives a low-code Power Query experience with a large set of connectors, which suits analysts. Notebooks and stored procedures need code.

questions.stem: A transformation must process several terabytes of semi-structured files and call Python libraries for parsing. Which tool fits best?

options.text: A T-SQL view
Dataflow Gen2
A deployment pipeline
A Spark notebook

questions.explanation: Spark notebooks scale out over large data and can use any Python library, which suits big, complex transformations written by data engineers.

questions.stem: A team keeps its curated data in a warehouse and already writes its business rules in T-SQL. Where should the transformations from staging to curated tables run?

options.text: In a KQL update policy
In a Spark notebook that rewrites the warehouse files directly
In stored procedures in the warehouse
In a Dataflow Gen2 that exports to CSV

questions.explanation: When data lives in the warehouse and the team works in T-SQL, stored procedures there keep the work in one engine and one language. Moving T-SQL rules into Spark or a dataflow would add a second engine and language for no gain.

questions.stem: Which two are reasons to choose a notebook over Dataflow Gen2 for a transformation? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: The team wants to write Power Query M
The data volume needs distributed processing
The logic needs custom Python libraries
The source is one small spreadsheet
The authors want a no-code visual editor

questions.explanation: Notebooks win on scale and on access to code libraries. A visual no-code editor, Power Query M and small simple sources all point to Dataflow Gen2.

questions.stem: Business users must apply custom cleanup steps to source data before it's ingested into a Fabric warehouse, and they don't write code. Which ingestion option fits?

options.text: A pipeline Copy activity with column mapping
A Dataflow Gen2 with the warehouse as its destination
The COPY INTO statement
A CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statement

questions.explanation: Dataflows give a code-free experience with custom transformations before ingestion. COPY INTO and CTAS are T-SQL, and the Copy activity only does lightweight transformations such as type conversion and column mapping.

questions.stem: A warehouse transformation joins a table with a CSV file in ADLS Gen2 through OPENROWSET, and several other procedures read the same file every day. What should you do to improve performance?

options.text: Convert the warehouse table to a CSV file next to the source file
Replace the join with a Dataflow Gen2 that reads the file on every refresh
Read the file through OPENROWSET again in each procedure
Ingest the file into a dedicated warehouse table and join to that table

questions.explanation: Reading through OPENROWSET can be slower than reading a table, so external data that's accessed repeatedly should be ingested into a dedicated table.

questions.stem: A SQL team writes all its logic in T-SQL. It must load Parquet files from ADLS Gen2 into a warehouse table as part of a stored procedure, with the highest ingestion throughput. What should it use?

options.text: The COPY statement
A Dataflow Gen2 started from the procedure
A notebook that writes the files to the warehouse
An INSERT ... SELECT from a lakehouse shortcut, run row by row

questions.explanation: COPY is the code-rich option with the highest ingestion throughput, and it can be part of T-SQL logic. It supports CSV, JSONL and Parquet from ADLS Gen2, Blob Storage and OneLake.

questions.stem: Which two statements about Dataflow Gen2 are true? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: The DataflowStaging items should be deleted once the first dataflow is published
A published dataflow must be refreshed by hand, because Dataflow Gen2 can't be scheduled
New Dataflow Gen2 items are created without CI/CD and Git support unless you opt in
The first dataflow in a workspace creates background staging items that are shared by all dataflows and shouldn't be deleted
When you set a lakehouse destination, you choose whether to append new data or replace what's there

questions.explanation: The destination offers Append or Replace, and Fabric creates shared background Lakehouse and Warehouse items that shouldn't be deleted. Scheduled refresh is supported, and new items have CI/CD and Git support by default.

questions.stem: Put the steps of building a first Dataflow Gen2 that counts orders per customer and loads the result into a lakehouse in order.

options.text: Get data from the source and select the Orders and Customers tables
Create a new Dataflow Gen2 item in the workspace
Turn on scheduled refresh
Publish the dataflow
Group the Orders table by CustomerID with a count of rows
Set the lakehouse destination and choose Append or Replace

questions.explanation: You create the item, get data, transform it, set the destination, then publish. The dataflow is ready to refresh only after publishing finishes, so you schedule refresh last.

questions.stem: A SQL developer must build a reporting table in a warehouse by joining a warehouse table with a lakehouse table in the same workspace, using only T-SQL. What should they use?

options.text: COPY INTO pointed at the lakehouse table
A notebook that reads both tables and writes the result
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT with three-part names for the lakehouse table
A OneLake shortcut from the warehouse to the lakehouse Files folder

questions.explanation: CTAS, INSERT...SELECT and SELECT INTO can read tables in other warehouses and lakehouses in the same workspace. A notebook isn't T-SQL, and COPY INTO loads files, not tables.
